items.prompt: "Either we commit to showing up every single week from now on, or we admit game night is over." What's wrong with this, specifically?
choices: Nothing — those genuinely are the only two options once attendance dips
It's a false dichotomy — it presents two options as exhaustive while excluding real alternatives, like a reminder text, rotating hosts, or accepting an occasional miss
It's a straw man, because it misrepresents what someone else said
It's an appeal to authority, because it sounds like a rule being enforced
items.explanation: A false dichotomy specifically claims a possibility space is exhausted by two options when it isn't. Here, a reminder text, rotating who hosts, or simply accepting a one-off miss are all real alternatives the framing silently excludes.
items.reference:
🔀 False dichotomy — only two options claimed, a third exists
🎭 Straw man — refutes a distorted version of the claim
👤 Ad hominem — attacks the person, not the claim
🎓 Appeal to authority (misused) — cites unrelated/overbroad expertise
📉 Slippery slope — claims a cascade with no shown mechanism

Why: the group-chat message ruled out a reminder text, rotating hosts, and accepting an occasional miss — real options it never named or excluded on their merits.

items.prompt: Someone proposes "maybe we just need a reminder text before game night." The reply is "so you want us to guilt-trip anyone who's ever busy?" What fallacy is this?
choices: Slippery slope, because it predicts escalating guilt
Straw man — the reply argues against 'guilt-tripping busy people,' a much more extreme claim than the reminder text that was actually proposed
Ad hominem, because it's aimed at a person
This is a fair, accurate restatement of the original proposal
items.explanation: The original proposal was narrow and low-stakes (a reminder text). The reply substitutes a much harsher, easier-to-object-to claim (guilt-tripping busy people) and argues against that instead — the actual proposal never gets addressed.
items.reference:
💬 Real claim: "send a reminder text"
🎭 Reply attacks: "guilt-trip anyone who's busy"
❌ The gap between them is the straw man

Why: a straw man only works by swapping in a more extreme claim than the one actually made — the reply never engages the real proposal.
items.learnMore:
Spotting a straw man
StepWhat to check
1What was the actual claim, word for word?

The fix isn't just naming it — it's restating the real position precisely, the way a straw-man target should respond: 'that's not what I said, I said X.'

Treating any pushback as a straw man. If the reply accurately restates the claim and then disagrees with it, that's real disagreement, not distortion.

items.learnMore:

Example

items.prompt: Per L2's `isFalseDichotomy` function, what determines whether a claimed set of options is a false dichotomy?
choices: Whether the claim uses the words 'either' or 'or'
Whether the actual possibility space contains at least one option not covered by what was claimed as exhaustive — if every real possibility is named, it's not a false dichotomy at all
Whether more than two people disagree with the claim
Whether the claim was made under pressure or in an argument
items.explanation: The function's logic is exactly the definition: check whether any real possibility exists outside the claimed set. If `actualPossibilities` only contains what was already claimed, `isFalseDichotomy` correctly returns false — the dichotomy was genuine.
items.reference:
actual.some(p => !claimed.includes(p))

Why: a false dichotomy is exactly "a real option exists that the claim didn't name" — this is the whole check, expressed directly.
items.learnMore:
Making the check concrete
claimedOptionsactualPossibilitiesResult
[commit, quit][commit, quit, remind, rotate]true — false dichotomy
[succeeded, failed][succeeded, failed]false — genuine dichotomy

Turning a vague objection into a concrete check is the whole point: instead of arguing in the abstract about whether something's exhaustive, you can just list the real alternatives and compare.

Common mistake

Assuming a longer 'actualPossibilities' list always means a false dichotomy. If every extra item is nonsense or not actually feasible, it isn't a real excluded option.
